answer.headline: ORD weather-delay minutes per arrival exceed ATL by {F3} over the reporting-carrier window
answer.body: Over {F2.period}, calculated weather delay minutes per operated arrival were {F2} at ORD and {F1} at ATL. ORD exceeds ATL by {F3}, which is {F4} higher than the ATL rate. These values are {F2.class}: weather-cause minutes divided by operated arrivals for domestic reporting carriers. They are not observed raw totals and they are not forecasts.

claims.text: Over {F2.period}, weather delay minutes per arrival at ORD were {F2}.
Over {F1.period}, weather delay minutes per arrival at ATL were {F1}.
ORD minus ATL on this metric is {F3}, which is {F4} higher than the ATL rate.
Within the domestic reporting-carrier sample, ORD shows a higher weather-coded delay per arrival than ATL over the same window.

assumptions: The reporting-carrier window is the full On-Time arrivals coverage span, {F1.period}.
ORD is Chicago Ohare International Airport. ATL is Hartsfield Jackson Atlanta International Airport. The spelled Atlanta name did not resolve; the code ATL matched that airport alone.
limitations: On-Time data cover domestic flights of reporting carriers only. International flying and non-reporting carriers are outside these rates.
The metric uses only the weather cause code. Minutes coded to NAS, the carrier, or late aircraft, and cancellations, are not included, so this is not all weather-related disruption.
The comparison does not establish a cause. Weather severity, airline coding practice, and schedule mix are not identified.
Unmet demand, terminal capacity, fares, and profitability are not measured by these data.
Coverage versus T-100 passenger departures, shown with the evidence, uses overlapping months only and therefore stops short of the final month in {F1.period}.
Each rate is the window sum of weather-delay minutes divided by operated arrivals. This comparison does not establish the gap in each month.
